title: Which voice is yours
hookLine: of all the elders' songs, one sounds like you
carry: each kept in its own temper

cards: Ah, what bliss. I was vain. Fortunate both ways.
It occurs to me. So it is. Five lines from one week, and no two of them sound alike.
A former ruler sighing under a tree. A half-brother confessing. A son counting his blessings.
A poet who couldn't sit on a poem. An old teacher agreeing that he's old. The elders' songs aren't one voice.

teach.b: First, the voices that confess. Nanda: I was given to adornment. Uttama, among the sisters, left her cell again and again before the day she stayed.
Talaputa, the actor, argues with his own restless mind: when will it be? These songs start with the trouble and don't hide it.
Second, the voices that delight. Bhaddiya, once a ruler with guards inside and outside his palace, now sits at the root of a tree, unafraid: ah, what bliss. Mahakassapa loves his rocky hills.
Subhuti tells the rain to go ahead and fall.
Third, the voices that grieve and turn. Ananda after the passing, every direction dark. Kisa Gotami, praising good friends, then telling her grief, then the deathless.
Patacara, drawing down a lamp's wick with a needle.
Fourth, the plain voices. Mutta, glad to be free of the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband. Ambapali, her hair once black.
Rahula, counting what he inherited. Sona, taught by a lute, not too tight. No one in these collections is asked to sound like anyone else.
Each song keeps its singer's name and its singer's temper. The tradition kept the delighted and the mourner, the poet and the penitent, side by side.
So the question isn't which voice is best. It's which one you'd recognize if you heard it across a room.

how: The Theragatha and Therigatha keep each poem under its singer's name, so a reader can come back to one voice at a time.

o: a story of a past life

games.q: the elders' voices: tap the pairs.
p: ah, what bliss, under a tree
free of mortar, pestle and husband

s: the elders' songs all speak in one calm voice
they confess, delight, grieve and speak plainly, each in its singer's own temper.
each song is kept under its singer's name
the collections keep the name with the verses: Nanda, Mutta, Ananda, Ambapali and the rest.
the collections leave the grieving songs out
Ananda's verses are kept: every direction dark.

games.q: you're one of the monks keeping the elders' songs. Nanda's opens with a plain confession: I was given to adornment. what do you do with it?
o: leave it out: it doesn't flatter him.
soften it into something more dignified.
keep it as he said it, under his name.
games.why: the Theragatha keeps Nanda's confession as it stands, under his name, beside songs of delight and grief.

practice: Let the singers pass by one at a time, the confessor, the one in the hills, the mourner, the plain speaker, and notice not the one you'd like to be but the one you already sound like on an ordinary day.
Recall one line of that song as closely as you can, and let it repeat slowly in time with the breath; if two voices come, let them take turns.

wordCard.voice: Gatha. A verse: what the elders' songs are built from, a crowd of named voices confessing, delighting, grieving, speaking plainly, each kept in its own temper. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali gatha: a verse. Theragatha and Therigatha are the verses of the elder monks and the elder nuns.

carryVoice: Your line: each kept in its own temper. No singer had to sound like anyone else. That's day eight hundred twelve.
